What does “Use device session calories” do?
Glycogo starts from the calorie value reported by your synced device or platform (Garmin, Strava, Wahoo, Intervals.icu, and similar), then converts it to net active calories for fuelling targets.
Glycogo estimates session burn using your sport settings (for example cycling power, running pace, swim pace, efficiency preferences, and body weight) instead of the device number.
Even with device calories enabled, Glycogo will still likely show a lower figure than your watch. The app removes the resting portion of the device estimate to avoid double adding this expenditure.
Why do workout calories in Glycogo differ from my Garmin, Wahoo, or Strava?

During exercise your body draws energy from resting metabolism and from the work your muscles perform. Sports watches usually report the combined total. Glycogo separates the active portion so it is not counted twice, because your daily meal targets already include your general daily needs.

, which can pull planned and completed workouts from major fitness platforms. Imported sessions drive pre-session, during-session, and recovery fuel targets for that day.
You can also add or edit sessions manually inside the app.
How should I rate my session RPE?
When you add or edit a session manually, rate the
overall difficulty of the whole workout
on the Borg CR100 scale (1–100). This is session RPE: how hard the entire session felt relative to what you could maximally sustain for ~1hr, not the peak effort of your hardest interval.
A long aerobic ride with a few surges usually rates lower than a steady threshold block, even if peak power or pace was high.
As you move the slider in the app, a short label updates (for example “Moderate”, “Strong”, or “Very Hard”) to match the CR100 bands:
If you log intervals, warm up and cool-down as one session, the easy sections and recoveries between reps should lower the overall rating compared with your hardest rep.

When a workout is synced, Glycogo estimates training load (shown as RPE 1–100) from the activity data. It uses the best available metric first rather than requiring you to manually enter effort.

Within-day energy availability tracks your hour-by-hour balance between what you eat and what you burn as the day unfolds.
Many apps only look at your total at the end of the day. Glycogo focuses on

you are in deficit, because prolonged low-energy periods during the day are linked to hormonal disruption and poorer recovery and body-composition outcomes, even if a large evening meal brings the daily total back to balance.
What does the within-day energy availability timeline chart show?
The timeline is your within-day energy picture, showing both projected and logged meals, training sessions, and how your cumulative balance changes through the day.

Meal and session markers are interactive: hover or tap for details. The chart highlights when you spend extended time in a notable energy deficit, and helps you adjust meal timing or size to optimize energy levels over the day.
Why does the app show a deficit when I first wake up?

Your body keeps burning energy overnight for temperature regulation, brain function, and repair. Glycogo uses a circadian model that spreads resting metabolism unevenly across the day (less overnight, more during active hours) rather than dividing it equally across 24 hours.

The negative balance you see in the morning reflects overnight energy use and gives a realistic starting point for within-day fuelling. It is expected and not a sign that something is wrong with your settings.
What should my carbs-per-hour range be?
Your lower and upper bounds should reflect gut tolerance, training experience, and session demands:
Easy aerobic, recovery, or low-intensity, shorter-duration work. A common starting range is roughly 30-50 g/hr to support stable energy without overloading the gut.
Hard intervals, threshold work, or race-specific sessions where glycogen use is high.
Up to about 90 g/hr is a widely used upper guideline for sustained hard exercise (ACSM guidelines).

Some athletes tolerate and use more than 90 g/hr, especially when total energy demand is very high or when staying fuelled across long or multi-session days. Higher intakes often need deliberate gut training in practice. You can raise your upper limit as needed or as you adapt.
What should my minimum session duration be?
This setting controls when Glycogo adds
carbohydrate targets. Lowering the threshold adds during-session fuel to shorter workouts. Raising it keeps fuelling focused on truly long efforts.
, which suits most endurance training, with 60–90 minutes a good range. Shorter sessions often do not need intra-workout carbs.
What is the high-carb fuelling setting for a session?

on an individual workout, Glycogo always includes during-session carbohydrate targets for that session at the upper end of your carbs/hr range, even if it is shorter than your minimum duration setting or at a lower intensity.
This is useful for gut training (practising higher carb intakes in training) or when pre-session fuel is limited and you still need on-the-go carbohydrates during the workout.

Daily carbohydrate targets then combine your baseline meals with the total added from all sessions on that day.
What is the “Carb Load” setting used for?
Carb loading increases your baseline daily carbohydrate target for a chosen day to support fuller muscle glycogen stores before a key event or long effort.

Training on a carb-load day still adds session fuel on top of the elevated baseline. If you also have a workout that day, consider the lower end of your carb-load range so the total goal stays practical.
Why does the app schedule a pre-session snack?

Pre-session snacks help top up carbohydrate stores, which can be added for training before breakfast, or before hard or long work. By default the app places this about an hour before your session starts. You can change the timing or turn pre-session snacks off in settings.
What effect does pre-session snack timing have?
The timing setting controls how many minutes before your session the pre-session snack is scheduled, and how much carbohydrate is able to be placed in that slot.
Shorter gaps use a lower carb cap, whilst longer gaps allow more. This reflects sport nutrition guidelines on how much fuel is practical to absorb before hard work without overloading the gut.
If the pre-session target would exceed this cap, the excess calories and carbohydrates spill over to your other meals.
Why did my default meal times shift after I added a workout?

If your meal’s default time in settings (for example Breakfast at 07:30, Lunch at 12:30, Dinner at 18:30) falls within a workout session block, Glycogo automatically shifts it to avoid overlap and ensure adequate digestion time.
The meal is moved to either
directly to the end of the session
, selecting whichever option is closest to the meal’s original default time.
How does Glycogo handle multiple workouts on the same day?
Each session gets its own pre-session, during-session, and recovery nutrition timing. Net training energy and carbohydrate needs for the day reflect the combined load from all sessions.
Can Glycogo plan race day itself, as well as the days around it?

that turns your targets into a plan for the race itself, block by block: how much carbohydrate and fluid to take in during each segment, what to use at each aid station, and how your sweat rate and the conditions adjust the totals.
You can import a planned race from

What is the fueling heat map on the settings screen?
It shows how your planned carbohydrate intake per hour varies with session duration and RPE. Use it as a visual guide to how fuelling ramps up as efforts get longer or harder.
Use it alongside your carbs-per-hour bounds to check that easy and hard sessions produce targets that match your training and gut tolerance.
What if I do not know my FTP, critical pace, or swim CSS?

Leave those fields blank or at zero and Glycogo falls back to standard sport-specific estimates scaled to your body weight. You still get a usable calorie and fuelling range; entering personal benchmarks later will refine it.
What if I do not know my efficiency for cycling, running, or swimming?
Leave the efficiency sliders at their defaults. They represent typical values for each sport. You do not need lab testing to start using Glycogo.
Default reflects a typical gross efficiency for trained riders. Move left if you are newer to cycling or a more fast-twitch dominant athlete, and vice versa.
Default reflects a typical economy. Less economical runners need more fuel at the same pace; well-trained, economical runners need less.
Default reflects typical propulsive efficiency in the water. Less efficient technique or higher drag means higher calorie needs at the same pace.
You can adjust these settings over time based on feel, recovery, and performance.
How does cycling efficiency affect calorie burn?
Cycling efficiency describes how much of your total energy output reaches the pedals as mechanical power:
More energy is lost as heat for the same power, so calorie burn is higher.
Less total energy is needed to hold the same power, so calorie burn is lower.
Adjust the slider in settings if your real-world fuelling feedback suggests your defaults are too high or too low.
How does running economy affect calorie burn?

Running economy works on the same principle as cycling efficiency. It reflects how much energy you spend to sustain a given pace. Less economical runners burn more calories at the same speed; more economical runners burn less.
Why is swimming calorie estimation sensitive to technique and pace?

Water creates far more resistance than air. Small increases in speed can demand a disproportionately large rise in effort, and technique has a big impact on how much energy is spent fighting drag and staying aligned in the water, so calorie burn should not be based on speed alone.
Glycogo’s swim settings let you account for your personal efficiency. If you are unsure, start conservative and adjust based on how sessions feel and recover.
How does Glycogo work out how much fat and carbohydrate I am burning?

From the intensity of the session and your own inputs, using published group-level relationships between exercise intensity and substrate oxidation. In the lab, the fuel mix is measured by indirect calorimetry: the ratio of CO₂ produced to O₂ consumed (RER) indicates whether the energy is coming from fat or carbohydrate, and that research gives the expected fat and carbohydrate oxidation rates for a given intensity, body size, sex, age, and carbohydrate availability.

Glycogo applies those relationships to the session, so the fat and carbohydrate split shifts with how hard you are working. The exact model and its coefficients are proprietary, and because the relationships are group-level rather than individual measurements, treat the fuel mix as a planning estimate rather than metabolic testing.
When you log or plan foods, Suggest quantities recommends portion sizes to help close your remaining macro gaps for that meal, especially carbohydrates and calories, without manual trial and error.
What are meal templates and the meal builder?

Templates let you save combinations of foods you eat often and reload them in one step. The meal builder stages foods before you log them to a meal, so you can search, scan, or add items, edit amounts, and review the full meal before logging.
What happens when I mark a meal complete?
Marking a meal complete tells Glycogo you have eaten what you logged for that meal. That meal’s targets lock to your intake, and any remaining calories and macros for the day are
across your still-open meals using your meal distribution settings.
Your within-day timeline and projections update too, so the rest of the day reflects logged intake.
Why would I choose to hide calories?
Hiding calories keeps the focus on
instead of calorie totals. Many athletes find that useful when they want to fuel for training and recovery without calorie counting as the main scoreboard.

When enabled, kcal numbers are hidden across the home day view, meal cards, food search, and related charts, while carb/protein/fat targets and logging still work as usual. You can turn it back on any time from the home screen eye symbol control.

Why does the glucose:fructose ratio matter?

Gut absorption of glucose alone tops out around 60 g/h because it relies on a single transporter (SGLT1). Fructose is absorbed through a separate transporter (GLUT5), so pairing the two allows higher total intake and faster absorption, down to a floor of 1:0.8 at 120 g/h and above.

Two parts glucose (or glucose polymers such as maltodextrin) to one part fructose, the classic multiple-transportable-carbohydrate blend used in endurance research. It supports intakes above ~60 g/h and is the most common ratio across energy gels, chews, and drink mixes.
A higher-fructose blend used at the top end of intake (120 g/h and above), where research points to a floor around 1:0.8. Products such as SiS Beta Fuel and Maurten Gel 100 use this ratio.
How many carbs per hour should I aim for?

It depends on session duration and intensity. Around 60 g/h covers longer easy sessions; 60–90 g/h is a common race range; up to 120 g/h suits sustained hard efforts if gut-trained. Below ~60 g/h, glucose alone is usually sufficient and fructose is optional.
Are whole foods as good as energy gels?

Many whole foods have favourable glucose:fructose splits: dates and ripe banana are near 50/50, raisins 52/48, honey 47/53, so they can replicate the same ratios. Practical downsides are bulk, fibre, and batch variability compared with engineered gels.

substrate: Fat vs Carb Utilization Calculator - Substrate Fuel Mix by Intensity | Glycogo

See how your substrate utilization shifts with intensity: the grams of fat and carbohydrate your body burns per hour at every effort level, shaped by your fitness, the session, and what you ate. The carb vs fat curves are computed live by the same engine that powers the Glycogo app.
Pick an intensity axis & athlete profile
Borg CR100 scale (1–100) mapped through the Glycogo load-zone equivalency table.
Fat vs carb utilization by intensity
Press Calculate (or change an axis/athlete setting) to update the curves.

Substrate use during exercise is quantified by indirect calorimetry: because fat and carbohydrate oxidation yield different volumes of CO₂ per litre of O₂ consumed, the non-protein respiratory exchange ratio (RER = VCO₂ / VO₂) identifies the fuel mix. RER 0.70 corresponds to near-exclusive fat oxidation, RER 1.00 to near-exclusive carbohydrate, and RER ≈ 0.85 to an even energy split (Peronnet & Massicotte, 1991). Each point on the chart is reported as an implied RER with matching carbohydrate and fat oxidation rates in grams per hour, converted with non-protein energy equivalents (carbohydrate ≈ 4 kcal/g, fat ≈ 9 kcal/g).

As relative intensity rises, catecholamine drive, type-II motor-unit recruitment, and the energy rate demanded per unit of muscle shift supply toward muscle glycogen and blood glucose, and the relative fat contribution falls: the classic “crossover” (Brooks & Mercier, 1994; Romijn et al., 1993). In trained athletes, absolute fat oxidation commonly peaks around 45–65 % VO₂max (the “fatmax” zone), although with substantial individual variation (Achten & Jeukendrup, 2003).

Substrate availability influences oxidation. Pre-exercise and during-exercise carbohydrate raise carbohydrate oxidation at a given intensity; habitual carbohydrate intake and training status reshape glycogen stores and oxidative capacity; low-carbohydrate availability raises the relative fat contribution (Romijn et al., 1993; Burke et al., 2011). The model further adjusts for session duration, sex, age, and body mass, reflecting the group-level effects quantified in modelling analyses of submaximal exercise (Rothschild et al., 2022).
70 kg, male, 34 years, moderate-carbohydrate diet (4.0 g/kg CHO, 1.5 g/kg fat daily), 60-minute session at ~600 kcal/h. The production model returns:
For this athlete the 50/50 crossover (RER ≈ 0.85) falls near RPE 33 on the CR-100 scale; lower carbohydrate availability would move it toward higher intensities.

The interactive readout also reports the model’s implied RER at each point. Because the model maps fuel split to RER through a smooth physiological response curve rather than the strictly linear non-protein approximation, its implied RER can sit up to a couple of hundredths off the linear non-protein table (a little below near 90 % carbohydrate, a little above at the top of the range); the static table therefore lists only the internally consistent energy split and oxidation rates.

Outputs are group-level predictions of substrate partitioning for the inputs you supply, not measurements of your metabolism. Day-to-day variability, training status, diet history, heat, and gut tolerance all move real-world values. Use the explorer to compare scenarios and structure fueling, not as metabolic testing.

What is RER and what does RER 0.85 mean?

RER (respiratory exchange ratio) is the volume of CO₂ exhaled divided by O₂ consumed, the core measurement of indirect calorimetry. RER 0.70 ≈ 100 % of energy from fat, RER 1.00 ≈ 100 % from carbohydrate, and RER ≈ 0.85 marks an even 50/50 energy split. The chart’s RER readout is the model’s implied RER at that point.
At what intensity does fuel use become 50/50?

It is athlete-specific. For the default reference athlete here (70 kg, male, 34 years, moderate-carbohydrate diet) the crossover sits near RPE 33 on the CR-100 scale (moderate). Higher carbohydrate availability shifts it toward lower intensities; low-carbohydrate availability or fat-adapted training shifts it higher.
Why does carbohydrate intake shift the curve toward carbohydrate?

Substrate availability influences oxidation. Pre-exercise and during-exercise carbohydrate raise plasma glucose delivery and reduce the relative reliance on fat at the same absolute intensity; habitual low-carbohydrate intake does the opposite. These are the acute and chronic effects the diet sliders reproduce.
Are the g/h numbers intake targets?

, what your body burns from muscle glycogen, blood glucose, and plasma fatty acids. Exogenous fueling targets (for example, 60–90 g/h of multiple-transportable carbohydrate during long sessions) are a separate prescription that only partially overlaps oxidation.

They apply group-level relationships from indirect-calorimetry research to the inputs you choose, so individual values vary with fitness, training status, diet history, and environment. Use the tool to compare scenarios and plan fueling structure; for individualised session fueling, the Glycogo app incorporates measured power, heart rate, and energy expenditure.

Four apps now do roughly the same job. Underneath they answer different questions, so the numbers they hand you will not match. Last checked 30 October 2026.

If you want your training to set your fuelling, there are four apps worth knowing about. Each one turns your sessions, body size and food into daily carbohydrate and calorie targets, fuelling for each session, and something for race day. On the surface they look interchangeable.

They are not. What separates them is where the targets come from, whether they use your own physiology rather than a population estimate, whether they show their workings, and what happens when a day does not go to plan. Below is the same set of rows filled in for all four, then the differences that actually change the numbers.

Most apps start with an estimated resting metabolic rate, add the cost of your sessions and turn the total into macro targets. It is a sound way to manage weight, and three of the four do exactly that. It does not tell you how much energy is left for everything other than training, relative to your fat-free mass: the number that matters for hormonal function, bone health and the low energy availability problems that build up quietly over a season.

Glycogo sets daily requirements from energy availability and training expenditure, then lets you set macro ranges and meal distribution around them, and tracks availability across the day: projected levels, the largest hourly deficit, and time spent below target. Hexis shows availability live through the day with Live Energy, worked from an estimated resting metabolic rate. Fuelin and Avitu do not compute it within the day at all.

Effort is not the same as cost. Two athletes can hold the same heart rate at very different metabolic costs, and the difference shows up in what a session takes out of you. Glycogo takes cycling FTP and gross efficiency, running critical speed and running economy, and swimming CSS with propulsive efficiency, then estimates the carbohydrate and fat each session uses. Hexis asks for FTP, critical speed and cycling efficiency, so cycling and running costs come from your physiology there as well, but running economy and swimming are left out. Fuelin takes FTP and threshold pace. Avitu takes FTP alone, so cycling has a threshold to work from while running and swimming do not. If you train on a power meter or a watch with a threshold estimate you trust, this is the part that moves the numbers most. What comes out of it matters as much as what goes in: only Glycogo turns those inputs into a per-session carbohydrate and fat split.
You can see the same engine on its own in the free
: grams of fat and carbohydrate per hour at every intensity, shaped by your fitness and the session.
Session carbohydrate, race day and the next day

Gut tolerance is individual, trainable and different by sport: 90 g/h on the bike is not 90 g/h running. Glycogo lets you set carbohydrate-per-hour ranges by sport and GI tolerance, or start from the recommended targets. Hexis and Fuelin apply a fixed hourly target that you cannot change in the app unless you are on a coached plan, and Avitu applies one you cannot change at all. That is fine until you are gut training towards something higher. The free
shows how a product or a mix of foods splits against the glucose to fructose ratios used in the research.

Race day is where a fuelling app either helps or gets in the way. Four hours on a rolling course is not the same as four hours on a climb, and where the aid stations fall decides what you carry. Glycogo plans by course profile and section, including the products you will use and the stations you will pass, with an 8 to 12 g/kg carb load you can switch on for the days before. Fuelin gives race week and race day guidance without course planning. Avitu sets carb loading and in-activity targets around a key event. Hexis has no in-app race planner.

The quieter difference is the next day. Glycogo lets you mark meals as completed and carries any shortfall or surplus into tomorrow's meal targets, so a light day on the bike is accounted for rather than quietly forgotten. Hexis and Fuelin allow meals to be completed but do not carry the difference forward. Avitu offers neither.

Glycogo's core features are free; Premium adds AI chat, voice, photo and barcode logging for about €3.50 or $4 a month. Hexis is €16.99 a month or €109.99 a year with no free tier. Fuelin is $29 a month or $139 a year with no general free trial, and is the most expensive of the four. Avitu is €4.99 a month or €49.99 a year with a 14 day trial that does not ask for a card. Prices are as displayed on 30 October 2026 and are set by each vendor, so check before you subscribe.

Coaching support, dietitian review, food database size, integrations beyond Intervals.icu and how pleasant each app is to use day to day. All of it matters, and none of it is comparable from public documentation. Nor does it rank the four: the right one depends on whether you want a weight management tool with fuelling attached, or a fuelling tool built from your own physiology. The table is there so you can check the specific thing you care about.
